title: Measuring with different units
keyIdea: To measure a length, lay the same unit again and again, end to end, with no gaps and no overlaps, and count. Measure the same thing with a different unit and you get a different number, but the thing has not changed length. A longer unit fits fewer times, so the number is smaller; a shorter unit fits more times, so the number is bigger. A scarf can be 3 straws long and also 12 paper clips long. A book is 28 centimetres but only 11 inches, because an inch is longer than a centimetre. Always say the unit with the number, and start a ruler at 0.
familyTip: Measure the same table twice: once with your hand spans and once with a spoon laid end to end. Before you start, guess: will there be more spans or more spoons? Then measure your bed with your feet, heel to toe, and ask a grown-up to do the same. Who counted more feet, and why?

visual.caption: Same thing, two units. Which gives lots of units, and which gives only a few? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: measure a scarf in straws then paper clips, stretch a unit to change the count, read cm and inches, find whose foot is longer.

kid: To measure how long something is, pick a unit, like a straw. Lay straws end to end along it. Do not leave gaps. Do not let them overlap. Then count them.

Now measure the same thing with paper clips. A clip is much shorter than a straw, so lots more clips fit. A scarf can be 3 straws long and 12 clips long. The scarf did not grow. Only the unit changed.
So a big unit gives a small number, and a small unit gives a big number. If you count more feet than your mum across the same rug, your foot is the shorter one.

A ruler has units that are all the same size. A centimetre is short. An inch is longer. A book is 28 centimetres but only 11 inches. Put the end of the thing on 0, and always say the unit, like 28 cm.
adult: Ages 7 to 8. US Common Core 2.MD.A.2 asks children to measure an object twice using length units of different lengths and to describe how the two measurements relate to the size of the unit. England's Year 2 programme of study asks them to choose and use standard units (cm and m) to estimate and measure length. Key words: unit, length, end to end, centimetre (cm), inch, ruler, measure, estimate.

The rule is an inverse relation: the length stays fixed, so the number of units times the size of one unit is the same each time. A 60 cm scarf is 3 straws of 20 cm or 12 clips of 5 cm. One inch is exactly 2.54 cm, so a 28 cm book is about 11 inches and an 18 cm pencil about 7 inches.

A common mistake is to think a bigger unit gives a bigger number, or that the count stays the same whatever unit you use. Other slips are leaving gaps or overlaps between units, starting a ruler at 1 instead of 0, and writing a number with no unit.

In the lab your child lays straws and then paper clips along a scarf, drags the size of a unit until a ribbon takes 6, 3 and 12 units, slides a book and a pencil to 0 on a ruler and reads them in centimetres and in inches, decides whose foot is longer from two foot counts, and checks a robot's claims.

practice.prompt: A plank is {a} straws long. A paper clip is a quarter of a straw, so 4 clips fit along 1 straw. How many paper clips long is the plank?
practice.hint: Each straw is as long as 4 clips. Count 4 clips for every straw.
practice.explain: {a} straws, and 4 clips for each straw: 4 × {a} = {=4*a} clips. The shorter unit gives the bigger number.

practice.prompt: A bench is {a} big blocks long. One big block is as long as 2 small blocks. How many small blocks long is the bench?
practice.hint: Every big block can be swapped for 2 small blocks.
practice.explain: 2 small blocks for each of the {a} big blocks: 2 × {a} = {=2*a}. Small units fit more times.

practice.prompt: Ben measures his desk in centimetres and then in inches. Which number will be bigger?
practice.hint: Which unit is shorter: a centimetre or an inch?
practice.explain: A centimetre is shorter than an inch, so more centimetres fit along the desk. The centimetre number is bigger.

practice.prompt: Lily lays paper clips along a book but leaves gaps between them. What happens to her count?
practice.explain: The gaps are part of the book but no clip covers them, so fewer clips fit. Her count is too small. Lay units end to end.

practice.prompt: A ribbon starts at the 2 on a ruler and ends at the 10. How long is it?
practice.hint: Count the centimetres from where it starts to where it ends.
practice.explain: From 2 to 10 is 8 centimetres. Reading 10 would only work if the ribbon started at 0.

pool.prompt: A rug is 6 of Dad's feet long and 9 of Amy's feet long. Whose foot is longer?
pool.hint: Fewer units fit when each unit is longer.
pool.explain: Dad needed fewer feet for the same rug, so each of his feet must be longer.

pool.prompt: A shelf is 4 rulers long. About how many pencils long could it be, if a pencil is shorter than a ruler?
pool.hint: Is the new unit longer or shorter?
pool.explain: A pencil is shorter than a ruler, so more pencils fit: more than 4. Seven pencils makes sense.

pool.prompt: Why do people use centimetres instead of hand spans to measure?
choices: Every centimetre is the same size
Hands are too small to use
pool.hint: Are everyone's hands the same size?
pool.explain: Hand spans change from person to person, so two people get different numbers. A centimetre is the same for everyone.

pool.prompt: A stick is 30 cm long. About how many inches long is it?
pool.hint: An inch is longer than a centimetre, so expect a smaller number.
pool.explain: An inch is about 2 and a half centimetres, so fewer inches fit: about 12 inches.

pool.prompt: Omar says his pencil is 15. What should he add?
pool.explain: A number alone does not tell you how long. 15 cm and 15 paper clips are very different lengths.

pool.prompt: Jo lays cubes along a line, but some cubes sit on top of each other at the ends. Her count will be…
pool.hint: Overlapping cubes cover the same bit twice.
pool.explain: Overlaps mean some length is counted twice, so more cubes are used than needed. The count is too big.

pool.prompt: A path is 20 small steps long. Measured in giant strides, it could be…
pool.hint: Giant strides are longer than small steps.
pool.explain: Longer units fit fewer times, so the number goes down: 8 strides is sensible.

pool.prompt: Where should the end of a pencil go when you measure it with a ruler?
pool.hint: Where does the counting of centimetres start?
pool.explain: Put the end on 0, then read the number at the other end. Starting at 1 adds a centimetre that is not there.

pool.prompt: A rope is {a} metre sticks long. Half a metre stick fits 2 times along one metre stick. How many half-metre sticks long is the rope?
pool.hint: Each metre stick is as long as 2 half-metre sticks.
pool.explain: 2 half-metre sticks for each metre stick: 2 × {a} = {=2*a}. The shorter unit gives the bigger number.

pool.prompt: A table is {a} rods long. One rod is as long as 3 cubes in a row. How many cubes long is the table?
pool.hint: Swap every rod for 3 cubes, then count all the cubes.
pool.explain: 3 cubes for each of the {a} rods: 3 × {a} = {=3*a} cubes. The shorter unit fits more times.
